Selecting and arranging

Selecting shapes, finding them in the object list, aligning, mirroring, rotating, laying flat on a face and multiplying in patterns.

この章はまだ日本語になっていません。このあとは英語で書かれています。

Selecting

A click on a shape selects it. With Shift you add more or take them away again. While Shift is held and two or more shapes are selected, a small number below the mouse pointer counts them. A click on empty space clears the selection, and so does Esc. Drag a frame on the empty workplane to select everything it touches; with Shift held, the frame adds what was not selected and takes away what was. If you would rather pick one part out of a cluster, switch on 「枠をドラッグする向きで決める」 in the settings (area 「外観」): a frame dragged to the right then takes only what lies completely inside it, one dragged to the left still everything it touches, and its line is dashed. Hold Alt while you drag to turn the frame around for that one drag, for example to take whole bodies from the side where the direction would not allow it. And Ctrl+A selects all visible bodies. While you drag a body or a handle of the frame, Esc cancels as long as the mouse button is still held: everything goes back as it was, and nothing is added to the history.

A shape behind another one, such as a hole inside a body, you reach without turning the view: right-click the spot and choose 「ほかのものを選ぶ…」. The menu then lists every shape under the pointer, from front to back. The one your pointer is on is outlined in the view, even through the shapes in front of it; a click selects it, and with Shift it is added to the selection. The entry is there whenever more than one shape lies under the pointer; on a tablet, a long press opens the same menu.

What is in your way you hide (「選択を非表示」, Ctrl+H). Hidden shapes stay in the design, they are just not visible and stay out of the export; the export window says beforehand how many there are. Ctrl+Shift+H brings them all back. What should stay put you lock with the padlock at the top of the settings or with Ctrl+L. A locked shape cannot be moved, resized, turned, recoloured or deleted: its handles turn grey, a padlock shows beside the arrow on top, and the tools that would change it are greyed out. Hovering a handle still shows its sizes, and a key that would change it says "Object locked". While one locked shape is in the selection, nothing changes for the others either. Hiding, renaming, copying and duplicating still work. To keep a part as it is and still build with it, lock only its shape: the shield beside the padlock, 「Lock shape」 in the right-click menu, or Ctrl+Shift+L. It can still be moved, turned, lifted, lined up, copied and grouped with others, but its size, its settings and its name stay as they are: the handles that change its size are gone, the fields for them are greyed out, and resizing, mirroring, ungrouping, the edge tools and deleting are refused. A copy keeps the lock, and so does the part inside a group, which can then be moved and taken apart again but not resized. The object list has the shield as well, beside the padlock: a part whose shape is locked always shows it, the others show it on the selected row and under the mouse, and a click on it locks or unlocks the shape.

To work on a few parts deep inside a design, select them and choose 「Hide others」 in the right-click menu or under 「表示オプション」: everything else is hidden in one step, so Ctrl+Z or Ctrl+Shift+H brings it back. 「Invert selection」 in the right-click menu selects every visible shape that was not selected and lets go of the ones that were. Both are in the command search (Ctrl+K) as well, where you can also give them a key of your own.

A number on the button of the group 「表示」 says how many shapes are hidden, and a click on it shows them all again. A design that is opened with hidden shapes says so once, with a button to show them. A part you hide while a group is open stays hidden when you close it with 「完了」: the group keeps its size and the parts left stay as they are, the hidden part still counts when the group is aligned, and showing all hidden shapes leaves it alone. Open the group again to show it.

The object list

With many parts it is easy to lose track in the view. The object list (「オブジェクトリストを表示」 or Ctrl+Shift+O) shows all shapes as a list. It stays open or closed as you left it, for every design, until you close it; the choice is kept in the browser.

  • A click on an entry selects the shape, including parts inside a group. With Shift held you add more entries or take them away again, just as in the view. The arrows fold groups open and shut.
  • The label shows whether a part is 「ソリッド」 or 「穴」.
  • Under the name stands what kind of shape it is. A body that is no longer a plain shape (rounded, hollowed or imported) says 「正確なボディ」 when the STEP export writes it exactly, and 「メッシュ」 when it is only triangles and goes as STL. A taper, lean or twist set after rounding or hollowing a body bends only its mesh, so it then says 「メッシュ」.
  • Padlock and eye lock and hide single parts.
  • 「名前を変更」 gives a part a name of its own; the pencil beside the name at the top of the settings does the same for the selected shape. Sensible names help enormously in larger designs.
  • The A–Z button in the title bar (「名前を付けた図形をA–Z順に並べる」) sorts the shapes you have named alphabetically, with numbers counted as numbers (Part 2 before Part 10). Shapes that still carry their default name stay below in the order you added them, the newest last, and parts inside groups are sorted the same way. Only the list changes, never the design. A second click shows everything in the order added again, and the browser remembers the choice.
  • The handle at the left of a row (six dots) moves a shape in the list: drag it up or down, or focus it and press ↑ or ↓. That changes the design's own order, the one the list returns to when the A–Z sort is off, and Undo takes it back. With the A–Z sort or a search on, the handles are hidden.
  • To put a shape into a group, fold the group open with its arrow and drag the shape by its handle onto the group's parts; the group gets an orange frame. The shape stays where it is and keeps its name, and so does the group: a group is merged again with it, a bundle just takes it in. The parts of a folded-open group have a handle of their own: drag one out of the group and it lies loose again, at the place in the list where you drop it, or drop it on another folded-open group to move it there. A group left with one part is gone and leaves that part. Undo takes each of these back in one step. While you are editing a group, this is off.
  • The search field finds shapes by name and by kind, so also "cylinder" or "hole". It also looks inside groups, however deeply nested: a group holding a match stays in the list and folds open to show the matching parts and the groups that lead to them. A group found by its own name shows all its parts when you open it.
  • The arrow on the far left of the title bar folds the list down to its title bar and back.

The list sits docked just right of the view cube. Drag it by its title bar to put it anywhere on the workplane; it passes underneath the view cube and the view bar. Drop it back beside the view cube, or double-click the title bar, and it docks again. Where it was and whether it was folded are remembered in this browser.

Typing a position

The card 「位置」 in the properties panel shows where the selected body stands, and you can type it: 「X」 and 「Y」 are the middle of its box on the plate, with the same signs as the distances shown on the workplane, and 「Z（高さ）」 is the height of its underside. With 「測るところ」 at the top of the card you switch to 「エッジ」: X and Y then show the body's left and front edges, so you put an edge exactly on a measure. The setting stays until you switch back to 「中心」. X counts to the right, Y towards the back and Z up, by the right-hand rule as in Tinkercad and CAD programs; the axis arrows on the plate show the directions. The values go in the unit you set, and the sliders reach as far as dragging does.

Parking parts beside the plate

You can drag a shape past the edge of the plate and leave it there, about one plate width beyond each side, to keep it for later. The arrow keys move it as far as you like. A parked part still belongs to the design and goes into the export with everything else. To leave it out, hide it or export only the selection. If you have picked a printer, layerling warns at export when something sits outside its plate.

Snapping while moving

When you drag a shape across the workplane, it snaps to other shapes: its left, right, front or back edge or its centre lands exactly on an edge or centre of another shape. A pink guide line shows what it is holding on to. That way two parts sit flush side by side or centred one behind the other without typing numbers. It works with the grid switched off, too. The centre of the workplane counts too: the pink lines show when the shape sits in the middle of the plate along X, along Y or both.

Hold Shift while dragging to keep the move on one axis: the shape follows whichever direction, X or Y, you have dragged further in, and leaves the other alone. Best press Shift once you are already dragging; on a shape that is not selected yet, a click with Shift only adds it to the selection.

Or pull the red or the green arrow on top of the selection: it moves along X or along Y only, and the shape follows the mouse along that line even in a low view, where a free drag runs off far. The arrows snap as a drag does, Alt lets go, and afterwards you can click the distance moved and type the exact value.

With Alt already held when the drag begins, you drag a copy, as in Tinkercad: the shape stays where it is and the copy lands where you let go. Pressing Alt only on the way pauses snapping; the shape then follows the grid only. A copy, too, snaps only once you let go of Alt on the way. To switch snapping off for good, use the grid menu in the bottom right (「シェイプにスナップ」) or the settings. For now only moving on the normal workplane snaps, not lifting and not resizing.

Aligning

Two or more selected shapes are lined up with 「整列」 (L, or right-click the selection and choose it): points appear around the selection for left, centre and right, front, centre and back, and top, centre and bottom. A click on a point moves all shapes there. If you first click one of the selected shapes, it stays in place and the others line up with it. A locked shape in the selection is that fixed shape by itself. Left, right, front, back, top and bottom go by the box round a shape; the centre of a triangle, a pentagon or a star is its own middle, so a hole centred on one sits in the middle of the shape and not of its box.

A shape turned at an angle, say by 45°, has its box round it to line up with, not its own edges. To line up with the edges, set a workplane on a face of that shape first (「作業平面を配置」, then click the face): the points then stand on the axes of that plane, and the shapes are measured and moved along them, as in Tinkercad. Reset the workplane to line up along the plate again.

The key is L. Esc cancels.

Matching sizes

Hold Alt while aligning and the dots turn into squares: a click no longer moves the shapes but changes their size. A dot at a side stretches each shape to that side, its other side staying where it is, as if you had dragged its handle there. The dot in the middle leaves each shape in its place and gives it the width, length or height in that direction. That way you swap a box for a cylinder of the same size, say, or replace a broken piece of a mesh with a clean shape. Move over a dot with Alt held and you see beforehand how large the shapes become.

The reference is the shape you clicked first; only the others change. Without one, the side dots stretch all shapes to the farthest side, and the middle dot gives them all the size of the largest. A cylinder stays round, so it grows in the other direction too. A shape turned at an angle stays as it is; shapes turned by 90° work.

Equal gaps

Beside the middle point of each line stands a wider dot with a bar on each side. It spreads three or more shapes in that direction so that the space between neighbouring edges is the same everywhere, whatever size each shape is. The first and the last shape stay where they are, the ones between move. A row of holes of different sizes gets the same wall between them, for example. Move over the dot and you see beforehand where the shapes go; the status bar then tells you the gap.

If a board (a base the others stand on, such as a flat box, not an SBC board) is among the selected shapes, longer in that direction than all the others, the shapes are spread on it: the gap at its edges is as large as the one between them, and a single shape comes to its middle. Shapes in several rows, such as the animals of a peg puzzle, are spread row by row; shapes whose boxes overlap across the direction form one row. Where the shapes stand in no clean columns, as the animals do from front to back, the shapes standing side by side move as a whole row instead. The whole puzzle then takes one click from left to right and one from front to back.

Without a board, hold Shift and click an empty spot of the plate first: the plate is then the fixed shape, equal gaps spread the shapes over the whole plate with the same gap to its edges, and the other dots line them up on its edges or its middle. Another click with Shift on the empty plate lets it go. A click on empty space without Shift ends Align, as L and Esc do.

Hold Alt and click the dot to type the gap yourself, say 5 mm: the shapes line up that far apart, starting at the first shape or at the one you clicked first; on a board the row comes to its middle. A locked shape stays where it is, so one between the outer shapes stops the equal gaps.

Mirroring

「ミラー」 (M, or right-click the selection and choose it) flips the selection across a plane: 「左右」, 「前後」 or 「上下」. Click the matching axis arrow. That is handy for symmetric parts: build one half, copy it and mirror the copy.

Rotating and setting the pivot

You rotate with the curved arrows on the shape, with the numbers in the settings or with R in 45° steps. When you drag on the rotation circle, the turn snaps to every tick, that is every 22.5°; hold Shift for finer steps, and extra ticks appear every 11.25°. Drag outside the circle to turn freely in 1° steps, or in 45° steps with Shift. Normally the selection turns about its centre. Sometimes it should not, for example when a tilted tube is to be turned further at its end. For that there is 「回転の中心を設定」: afterwards click on a face. A flat face supplies its centre, for example the axis of a tube end. On a group or a bundle the face runs on across parts that meet, as on one body, and the pivot goes to the middle of the whole face once the parts are joined, except on a group or bundle with text in it, or a bundle with a hole among its parts. The selection now turns about that point. A second click on the tool removes it again.

The angles stay with the body. In its settings, 「回転」 shows them as 「X軸まわり」, 「Y軸まわり」 and 「Z軸まわり（高さ）」, named like the position: Y runs across the plate, Z is up. Type an angle there and the body turns to it - about its centre, or about its own pivot if it has one. While a turned body is selected, its angles also show below it on the workplane; 「回転したボディの角度を表示」 in the settings switches that off.

With one body selected, the pivot belongs to that body: select other parts and come back, and it is still there. It moves, turns and scales with the body, is saved in the project and comes back with Undo. Under 「位置」 the pivot has its own X, Y and Z, which you can type or nudge, and 「削除」 takes it away. You can also drag the pivot's red marker with the mouse: it slides over the surface of the bodies and snaps to corners, edge midpoints and edges, so a hinge pin lands exactly on a corner. With several bodies selected the pivot is only for that selection, and a new selection removes it. Grouping or bundling them keeps it: the group takes the pivot as its own, with X, Y and Z under 「位置」. Hold Shift while dragging the red marker and it snaps to the centre of the face under the pointer instead - the axis of a round face, the middle of a flat one or the tip of a cone - looking through transparent bodies.

Laying flat on a face

Should a part lie on its best side for printing? Select it, click 「面を下にして平らに置く」 and then the face that should go down. While you move the pointer over the part, the face under it lights up, so you see which one you are about to pick; turn the view to check the other sides. The part turns so that this face rests on the workplane.

Two parts should meet face to face, or line up flush? Select the part that should move, click 「面を合わせる」, then click its face and after that the face of the other part. In the tool window, 「面と面を突き合わせ」 puts the faces against each other (back to back, touching), 「同じ平面」 lays them in one plane side by side; 「隙間」 leaves room between them, for example for clearance. 「合わせる」 moves the part: it turns the shortest way until the faces are parallel - not at all if they already are - and then slides only towards the other face, so it keeps its place sideways. The other part stays where it is, and one Undo takes it all back.

Holes on one axis: 「同軸」 lines up round faces instead: a hole over a hole, a pin in a hole, a screw in its clearance hole. Choose it before you click the faces. Then click the round inside of a hole (or the outside of a pin) on the part that moves, and a round face of the other part; the whole round face lights up while you point at it. 「合わせる」 turns the part the shortest way until the two axes are parallel and slides it straight across onto the other axis. Along the axis it stays where it was, so a pin keeps its height; push it in afterwards. This works on imported meshes too, as long as the hole is made of facets around one axis.

A point onto a point: 「Point to point」 moves the part straight, without turning it, so that one of its points lands on a point of another part. Click a corner, a spot on an edge, the centre of a round edge or a reference point on the part that moves, then the point where it should land; a dot shows which point the pointer would take. Under 「Move along」 switch off the axes it should not move along: with only X and Y on, the point ends up straight above or below the other; with only Z on, at the same height. One Undo takes it back.

Turning by a second and third pair: after 「合わせる」 the panel stays open for a second pair of points. The first point stays where it landed, marked in blue, and 「Turn」 turns the part about it until the line through its second point runs through the point you picked on the other part - so two edges come to lie on one line, even when the parts are not the same length. A third pair turns the part about the line through the two blue points until its third point faces the third point you picked, so the faces line up too - like aligning by three points in other CAD programs. 「Done」 ends it at any step; each step is one Undo.

An exact angle between two faces: 「面を合わせる」 leaves the faces parallel; there is no tool of its own for an angle between them, but this gets you there. First bring the faces together with 「面を合わせる」, so they are parallel. Then set the pivot on the edge where they meet (「回転の中心を設定」, click the edge or a corner) and type the angle, 15 or 30 say, in the 「回転」 card of the part. It turns about that pivot. The card's axes are the axes of the plate, so this works when the edge runs along X, Y or Z.

Just as simple are 「作業平面に落とす」 (D), which drops the selection onto the workplane, and 「作業平面の中央に置く」. With the workplane on a face, it centres on the point you picked with W and moves the selection only along that face, so what stands on it stays on it.

Alt+D drops several parts as one piece: they all go down by the same distance and so keep their heights to each other, while D drops every part on its own.

C picks the selection up, like Cruise in Tinkercad: it follows the mouse pointer and lies down on the face of another body you are over, sloped ones too. A click sets it down there, Esc leaves it where it was. Its underside then rests on the face, lined up with the face's edges as a new shape would be; it keeps its own turn about its up axis. Several parts travel together and keep their spacing. Over the empty plate, C stands a tilted part upright on the workplane again. Holding Shift while you carry sinks the part into the face instead: it stays upright, its top flush with the face and the body below it, which is how a countersink or a counterbore goes into a body; a new shape from the library is placed the same way with Shift held. Shift+D drops the selection with its top on the workplane instead of its base. Without a keyboard, the menu of a long press has 「面の上に置く」 for the same.

Patterns: row and circle

For hole grids, bolt circles and rings of teeth there is the 「パターン」. Select the shapes to be multiplied and click it in the ribbon.

  • 「一列」: The selection is repeated at equal distances. The row steps along all three axes at once, with 「間隔 X」, 「間隔 Y」 and 「間隔 Z（高さ）」: one of them gives a straight row, two or three a diagonal row or a staircase. A negative spacing lays the row the other way.
  • 「ボディ全体に並べる」: For holes along a plate, a key holder or a coat rack. Put the first piece on or into the body, choose 「Xに沿って」 or 「Yに沿って」 and set the 「端までの余白」: the original moves that far in from the nearer end (from the edge to the piece's side), and the last copy keeps the same gap to the far end. The spacing then follows the 「個数（元を含む）」: five holes or nine, they always fill the plate evenly.
  • 「Grid」: For the holes of a perforated plate or a field of equal pieces. 「Columns along X (with original)」 and 「間隔 X」 lay the columns side by side, 「Rows along Y (with original)」 and 「間隔 Y」 the rows from front to back. One column or one row gives a single line. A grid has at most 100 pieces; past that the rows are cut back, and the window says so.
  • 「円形」: The selection is spread around a centre. How many copies there are you set under 「個数（元を含む）」, and the 「全体の角度」 is 360° for a full circle. Choose whether the copies turn along. 「コピーごとの上昇」 lifts every copy a little more than the one before (a screw or an ascending spiral), and 「コピーごとの半径の変化」 moves it further from the centre or closer to it (a flat spiral); together they give a conical spiral. A spiral winds once around at most: an angle above 360° counts as a full circle, and there are at most 100 copies.

Tip: first set the pivot on a face with 「回転の中心を設定」, then the centre of the circle lies exactly there.

Afterwards the pieces keep the circle's centre as their pivot, also once grouped. That is where another part belongs, for example a ball in the middle of three legs: the middle of the pieces' box is not the centre, since three legs fill a box wider one way than the other. Right-click the pieces and choose 「回転の中心に印を付ける」, and the centre of the part you drag snaps onto it.

The copies first appear as a preview. Only 「作成」 creates them. If the copies are holes, group them afterwards with the body they should cut into.

With 「コピーをグループにする」 ticked, 「作成」 groups the original and all copies into one object in the same step, as 「グループ化」 would: a ring of 36 pieces is then one part you can move, colour or cut with. Above 5 pieces the box ticks itself; once you tick or untick it yourself, it stays as you set it. 「グループ解除」 brings the pieces back. If grouping does not work out, the pattern still comes in as separate pieces and the message says why.

Hole pattern on a face

For vents, speaker grilles, baskets and enclosures the 「穴パターン」 spreads holes evenly over a flat face or round the wall of a cylinder. You no longer have to make one hole, repeat it and set it onto the wall. Select exactly one body and click 「穴パターン」 in the 「変形」 group of the ribbon, next to the pattern. You can also right-click the body, or find it with Ctrl+K.

  1. Click a flat face of the body. The whole flat face around your click counts, not just the triangle under the pointer. The round wall of a cylinder, a tube or a bore works too, see below; any other curved face does not: you get a hint and click a flat one instead. On a group or a bundle a face runs on across parts that meet, as on one body; on a bundle only when no hole is among them. The parts are joined shortly after the tool opens; until then only one part's face lights up under the pointer, and a click waits for the join. On a group or bundle with text in it, only one part's face lights up, and the click joins the parts.
  2. In the window, set how the holes look and lie:
  • 「穴の形」: 「丸」, 「正方形」, 「長方形」, 「六角形」 or 「長穴」.
  • Size: the 「直径（Ø）」 of a round hole, the 「一辺の長さ」 of a square one, 「幅」 and 「高さ」 for a rectangle and a slot. For the hexagon the size is the 「対角の直径（Ø）」.
  • 「穴の角度」: rectangles and slots only: turns every hole in the face by that many degrees, counter-clockwise as you look at the face, from -90 to 90. The rows stay straight; if turned holes would come too close, even diagonally, layerling widens the spacing and the row spacing so a wall stays between them.
  • 「壁を貫く傾き」: flat faces only, not with a counterbore, countersink or own shape: slopes every hole through the wall, from -60 to 60 degrees. On a standing wall a positive slope puts the inner end higher, so rain runs back out. The size stays the hole's own, so it shows a little longer on the face; both ends of each hole keep the margin. A slope only hides the inside when the wall thickness times sin(angle) is at least the hole's height, so use low slots or a thicker wall for that.
  • 「Own shape」: repeats a shape from the scene in place of a hole: a rivet, a stud or the tread of a diamond plate. Choose it under 「Shape from the scene」. Its width and depth are the room it takes; it stands upright on the face as it was made, without its own turn. A body is set onto the face and joins it, a hole is cut in as deep as it is high. The shape itself stays where it is.
  • 「Hole type」: round holes only. 「Plain」 is a straight hole, 「座ぐり」 adds a pocket for a cap screw's head, 「皿穴」 a 90° cone for a countersunk screw. The size is then the 「軸の直径」; 「頭部の直径」 and, for the counterbore, 「頭部の深さ」 set the head. 「ねじサイズ」 fills them all in for a metric screw.
  • 「中心間の間隔」: the distance from one hole's middle to the next. If it is smaller than the holes allow, layerling raises it to the smallest possible value so a wall stays between the holes. For rectangles and slots it counts along the row, from left to right.
  • 「列の中心から中心まで」: rectangles and slots only: the distance from one row to the next. So narrow, tall holes stand close side by side while the rows keep apart. A hole 2 mm wide and 14 mm high needs 4 mm along the row and 16 mm from row to row with a 2 mm wall.
  • 「穴と穴の間の壁」: the same distance said another way: the wall left between two neighbouring holes, which is the wall thickness in the print. Set it and the spacing centre to centre follows (for rectangles and slots the row spacing too), and the other way round. For hexagons, rectangles and slots layerling measures the least distance between their edges.
  • 「配置」: 「格子」 puts the holes in rows and columns. 「千鳥」 shifts every second row by half a spacing and moves the rows closer, so every hole has neighbours at the same distance - with hexagons that makes a honeycomb.
  • 「Along the edge」: a ring of holes along the outer edge of the face instead, 「面のエッジからの余白」 in from it - screw holes round a lid or a plate. 「Spread by」 「Spacing」 keeps about the spacing, 「Number」 sets the 「Number of holes」; either way the spacing is evened out so the ring closes without a gap. 「A hole on every corner」 (on at first) puts a hole on each corner and shares every side out evenly between them. On a round face, or with the box unticked, the holes go evenly round from the top, and 「Start along the edge」 moves the whole ring along the edge.
  • 「面のエッジからの余白」: the clear distance between the holes and the edge of the face. Only holes that lie wholly inside the face minus this margin are made; anything that would reach beyond it is left out. The margin also holds around openings in the face.
  • 「深さ」: 「ボディ全体を貫通」 (the default) cuts through the whole wall. With 「カスタム深さ」 you give the depth in millimetres, for recesses, say.
  1. The holes show at once as a preview on the face and follow every value. The window says how many holes fit. 「別の面」 chooses another face, Esc closes the tool, and like the other tool windows it moves by its title bar.
  2. Only 「作成」 makes the holes.

The holes are ordinary holes grouped with the body, just as after 「グループ化」: nothing is baked in. 「グループ解除」 dissolves the group again and frees every hole, which you can then move, change or delete one by one. The whole thing is one step for 「元に戻す」. The tool does not make more than 400 holes at once; make the holes bigger or the spacing wider then.

The round wall of a cylinder, a tube or a bore takes holes too: a pen holder, a lamp shade, a tube with vents. Click the wall instead of a flat face; the whole wall lights up under the pointer. Every hole then points straight at the axis, and the rows go round the wall. On a wall that goes all the way round, each row holds a whole number of holes, evened out so the ring closes without a gap and never closer than the spacing; the window says how many go round and how far apart. The margin holds to the rims at the top and the bottom and to openings in the wall, on a part of a wall (a rounded edge, say) to its sides as well. 「壁を貫通」 cuts through the one wall you clicked and leaves the far side of a tube whole; on a solid cylinder the holes go in to its middle. Clicked inside a bore, the holes go outward through its wall. 「Along the edge」 is for flat faces and is not offered on a wall.

An AI can do the same through the MCP bridge with layerling_perforate_face (see the chapter AI with MCP).

Pushing a face out or in

For a thicker wall, a raised pad on a face or a pocket cut into it, the 「面」 tool works on one flat face. It works on an imported STL too, where there is no sketch to change. Select exactly one body and click 「面」 in the 「変形」 group of the ribbon, next to the hole pattern. You can also right-click the body, or find it with Ctrl+K.

  1. Click a flat face of the body. As with the hole pattern, the whole flat face around your click counts; a curved face does not work here, a round wall neither. On a group or a bundle the face runs on across parts that meet, as with the hole pattern.
  2. In the window:
  • 「向き」: choose 「外: 材料を足す」 for material standing on the face or 「内: ポケットを切る」 for a pocket cut into it. A pocket goes no deeper than the body behind the face; on a hollow body it can still reach the cavity.
  • 「面のエッジからの余白」: how far the new outline stays inside the face's edge. Going out, 0 takes the whole face, which makes a wall thicker. Openings in the face grow by the same amount.
  • 「角の半径」: rounds every corner of the outline, the inner ones too, so a sharp tip ends in an arc. A notch narrower than twice the radius closes, and a part of the face narrower than twice the inset and the radius together is left out.
  • 「深さ」: how far the new part stands out of the face, or how deep the pocket goes.
  • 「別のボディにする（グループにしない）」: with the switch on, the new part (or the hole of a pocket) is a body of its own beside the body instead of a group with it, so you can resize it, move it or use it to cut at once.
  1. The result shows at once as a preview and follows every value. 「別の面」 chooses another face, Esc closes the tool.
  2. Only 「作成」 makes it.

What the tool adds is an ordinary sketch body, grouped with the body unless 「別のボディにする（グループにしない）」 is on (then 「グループを編集」 has nothing to open, and the part is free): nothing is baked in. 「グループを編集」 opens the group, and 「スケッチを編集」 on the new part shows the outline it follows. On the top or the bottom of a plain sketch body - one area, not grouped, mirrored, tapered, twisted or leaning, and without a stroke, key ring, fillet or chamfer - that is the body's own outline, set in when it is built, so its lines and arcs stay exact wherever the CAD kernel can set them in, for the edge tools and the STEP export. Resized later, the part keeps its inset. On any other face, and on every face of an imported mesh, the outline follows the face's triangles, and a curve is made of short straight pieces. The whole thing is one step for 「元に戻す」. To change the inset or the radius later, undo and run the tool again. To round the top edge afterwards, use 「フィレット」 with 「上端のエッジ」 on the group as the last step: like every edge treatment on a group, it joins the group into one body.

An AI can do the same through the MCP bridge with layerling_push_face (see the chapter AI with MCP).

Changing several parts at once

With several parts selected, the properties panel on the right shows how many there are and offers what applies to all of them together: 「ソリッド」 or 「穴」, one colour for all (a click on 「ソリッド」 opens the colours) and the lock. With a mixed selection, one click makes them all solids or all holes. If any of the parts is locked, only the lock can be used. Sizes are changed with the handles, with 「パーセントで拡大縮小」 or by typing a number into a size label. With several parts the number is the size of the whole selection: every part grows with it, the spaces between them too, as when you drag a handle. Solid and hole also work with a right-click or the S and H keys.

Scaling by percent

To make one or several parts larger or smaller by the same share, say all the parts of a print file by 20 %, use 「パーセントで拡大縮小」. Select the parts, right-click them and choose 「パーセントで拡大縮小」, or search for it with Ctrl+K.

Under 「新しいサイズ」 you type the new size as a percentage of the current one: 120 % is a fifth larger, 50 % half the size. Width, depth and height change alike, so the proportions stay. The bottom stays where it is, so nothing sinks into the plate.

With several parts you choose how they grow:

  • 「まとめて」: The parts grow around their common centre, and the gaps grow with them. The whole becomes larger as if it were one part.
  • 「各パーツをその場で」: Every part grows where it stands, and the gaps between them stay the same.

The percentage field has the focus when the window opens, so from the keyboard it is Ctrl+K, the percentage, Enter; Esc closes the window. Only 「拡大縮小」 (or Enter in the field) changes the design, and one step back undoes it. With a locked part in the selection it does not open.

Undoing

「元に戻す」 (Ctrl+Z) and 「やり直す」 (Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y) step through your history. How many steps travel with the saved design you set in the settings under 「履歴」. Point at either button and its tooltip names the step it would take back or bring again, with the measure where the step has one, such as "Rounded the edges of Box (5 mm)" or "Moved 3 objects (12 mm)"; the message after the step says the same. To go back several steps at once, use the history view below. A message that reports a step just taken, such as "3 shapes deleted", has an Undo button that takes exactly that step back.

Looking back: the history view

「履歴」, next to undo and redo, opens a view of your history without changing anything. The work area shows the design as it was, and a slider at the bottom runs through every undo step: all the way to the right is the current state, each step to the left is one undo earlier, and states you have undone sit to the right of the current one. The arrow keys step through the states, Esc returns to the current state. The mouse wheel over the slider does the same, one state per notch, up to an earlier one; Page Up and Page Down jump ten states, Home goes to the oldest state and End back to the current one. You can turn and zoom the view meanwhile and click objects to bring them back (see below), but nothing can be moved; the design itself stays exactly as it is. If the bar covers something, drag it away by its title bar; a double-click on it brings it back. The list button in the title bar shows every step by name in a list, the newest at the top: a click on a step goes to that state, the state the design is at is marked 「現在」, and steps you have undone are grey. The list stays open the next time if you leave it open. The two play buttons under the slider run the history like a film: the one pointing right plays forwards from the state shown, the one pointing left plays backwards, each state for a moment, until the end; pressing the same button again pauses, and moving the slider, the wheel, the keys or the list takes over. Started at the end of its way, it begins again from the other end. 「Speed」 sets how long each state stays (slow, normal or fast) and is remembered for next time. Record the screen while it plays to show how a part came about.

Two things you can take along from an earlier state. 「この状態から新しいプロジェクト」 puts that state into a new design in the overview, named after this one with the time of that state in brackets - a design saved before layerling recorded times says "copy" instead - and with the history up to that point, so undo keeps working there. 「この状態をエクスポートする」 opens the usual export with that state as the design, so you can save it as STL, 3MF, STEP, a picture or a LYL file with the history up to that state.

You can also bring single objects back into the design. Click an object in the state shown - Shift+click adds more or takes one off again, a click on empty space picks nothing - and choose 「今のデザインに追加」. The view closes and a copy of each object lands in the current design exactly as it was in that state and at the spot it had there, selected, next to whatever the design holds now; nothing else changes. It is one step, so undo takes it back. Use it for a version of a part you changed since, or for one you deleted. A group comes back whole; notes and reference points on an object stay behind. Its name carries the time of that state, such as “Box (12:32)”, so it is easy to tell from the version the design has now. To bring back a part from inside a group, select the group and choose 「グループを開く」 or press E, as in the design: its parts are laid out where editing the group would put them, ready to pick, and the bar says which group you are in. 「外に出る」 closes it again. This is only to look - the group, the design and the history stay as they are.

「履歴を削除」 sits alone at the bottom left of the bar. After a question it removes every earlier step for good: the design keeps the state it has now (not the one shown), Undo has nothing to go back to and a file saved afterwards carries no history. Use it to share a design without its past, or to start the undo steps over. It cannot be undone; to share a file without touching your own design, choose 「なし」 when exporting instead.
